input.strategy_title: Feature Store as a supported RHOAI component
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Customers building recommendation and fraud models ask for a supported feature
store; today they self-manage upstream Feast next to the platform with no
lifecycle integration, no supported images, and no UI presence. Feast has a
Jira component reserved (Feature Store) but is not yet part of the platform:
there is no productized repository, no build pipeline, and no operator
integration. This strategy brings Feast in as a supported, installable RHOAI
component.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Administrators can enable a supported Feature Store (Feast) through the Platform Operator like any other managed component, with productized images. |
| HLR-2 | P1 | Data scientists can reach the feature store from workbenches with the Feast SDK preinstalled in at least one supported workbench image. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | The Dashboard shows the Feature Store as an enabled component and links users to its endpoints per project. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Product documentation covers enablement, a getting-started walkthrough, and supported limits. |

## Affected Components

- Feature Store
- Dashboard
- Platform Operator
- Documentation

## Out of Scope

- A feature-authoring UI in the Dashboard (link-out only this release)
- Managed offline-store infrastructure — customers bring their own storage

## Open Questions

1. Which Feast deployment topology do we productize first — the operator-based
   deployment or the standalone server per project? Upstream supports both;
   supportability differs.

# Productize the Feast operator-based deployment

## Description

Package Feast for the operator-based deployment topology (if that is the topology
selected by the Feast deployment-topology investigation): productized container
images and deployment manifests for the Feast operator and its operands, so the
Feature Store can be installed as a managed platform component.

## Scope

- Productized container images for the Feast operator and its operands, built from
  the midstream Feast repository through the Konflux build pipeline.
- Deployment manifests and RBAC for installing the operator on the platform.
- Validation of multi-project behavior of the operator-managed deployment.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Productized images for the Feast operator and operands build green through the
  Konflux pipeline.
- Deployment manifests install the Feast operator on a test cluster.
- Operator manages Feast resources across projects as designed.
- Images carry only license-cleared dependencies.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1: supported Feature Store with productized images, operator-based topology.

| existing_foundation | 1 | The Platform Operator and its enablement machinery already exist; this extends the component set. |
| open_questions | 1 | Topology is decided in this branch's favor before the epic starts. |

| architecture_claims | 0 | Platform Operator has no architecture-context file in this workspace; the strategy's claim that it is the existing enablement mechanism is taken from the strategy text and should be confirmed against the operator repository at implementation time. |

## Description

Wire the Feast operator-based deployment into the Platform Operator so administrators
can enable the supported Feature Store like any other managed component (if
operator-based deployment is the selected topology).

## Scope

- Disabling the component removes the managed resources cleanly.

  Operator, operator-based topology.

# Select the Feast deployment topology for productization

## Description

Resolve which Feast deployment topology RHOAI productizes first — the operator-based
deployment or the standalone server per project — and produce a decision record that
all downstream Feature Store, Platform Operator, and Dashboard work builds on. Upstream
Feast supports both; supportability differs, and the choice determines what gets
packaged, how administrators enable the component, and where per-project endpoints
come from.

## Scope

- Evaluate the operator-based deployment topology: deployment complexity, upgrade
  path, multi-project behavior, resource footprint, security posture, support surface.
- Evaluate the standalone-server-per-project topology against the same criteria.
- Validate both topologies in a test environment (a live OpenShift cluster).
- Document the decision: selected topology, rationale, rejected alternative, and
  consequences for Platform Operator enablement, per-project endpoint exposure, and
  Dashboard integration.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both topologies evaluated against a defined, written set of supportability criteria
  (deployment complexity, upgrade path, per-project isolation, failure modes,
  support surface).
- Both topologies exercised in a test environment; observations recorded.
- Decision record written naming the selected topology with rationale and the
  consequences for enablement, per-project endpoints, and Dashboard integration.
- Decision reviewed and agreed with stakeholders.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (gating): determines how the Feature Store is deployed and enabled as a
  supported component; every topology-dependent epic is blocked on this decision.

# Onboard the Feast midstream repository under opendatahub-io

## Description

Create the productized midstream repository for Feast under the opendatahub-io
organization so the platform can carry patches, build productized images, and run
release automation for the Feature Store component. Today Feast exists only upstream,
next to the platform, with no productized repository.

## Scope

- Fork/mirror upstream Feast into a midstream repository under opendatahub-io,
  following the conventions used by other RHOAI component midstream repositories.
- Set up branch strategy, OWNERS/maintainers, and CI trigger configuration.
- Document the upstream sync process.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Midstream Feast repository exists under opendatahub-io.
- Branch and release conventions match other RHOAI midstream repositories.
- Upstream sync process documented and executable.
- Repository accessible to the owning team and build automation.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1: productized repository foundation for the supported Feature Store component
  (no productized repository exists today).

# Validate licenses for Feast and the Feast SDK dependency tree

## Description

Run license scanning over the Feast codebase and the Feast Python SDK — including
transitive dependencies — to confirm both are usable in supported RHOAI productized
images and workbench images, and to surface any restrictions that must be documented
as supported limits.

## Scope

- License scan of the midstream Feast codebase (server, operator where applicable).
- License scan of the Feast Python SDK and its transitive dependencies as they would
  be installed in a supported workbench image.
- Review flagged licenses; record resolutions (acceptable, exclusion, remediation).
- Produce a go/no-go verdict and feed any restrictions into the documentation of
  supported limits.

## Acceptance Criteria

- License scans completed for the Feast codebase and the Feast SDK transitive
  dependency tree.
- Every flagged license reviewed with a documented resolution.
- Go/no-go verdict recorded; any usage restrictions handed to the documentation
  effort as supported-limits input.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1: licensing gate for shipping productized Feature Store images.
- HLR-2: licensing gate for preinstalling the Feast SDK in a supported workbench
  image.

# Preinstall the Feast SDK in a supported workbench image

## Description

Add the Feast Python SDK to at least one supported RHOAI workbench image so data
scientists can reach the feature store directly from their workbenches without
manual installation.

## Scope

- Add the Feast SDK (license-cleared, pinned version) to a supported workbench image
  definition.
